reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Field load tests provide the most reliable means of verifying the capacity of drilled shaft foundations. Types of tests include axial compression, axial uplift, and lateral load tests. Load tests serve multiple purposes: verifying design assumptions, calibrating site-specific design methods, and increasing AASHTO resistance factors to as high as 0.70 for static tests. The chapter covers planning, execution, instrumentation, and interpretation of field loading tests.
key_points: Load testing provides the most reliable verification of drilled shaft capacity
Types include static axial, bi-directional (O-cell), rapid (Statnamic), high-strain dynamic, and lateral
AASHTO resistance factors can be increased to 0.70 for statically tested shafts
Tests can verify design assumptions and calibrate site-specific methods
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft projects where load testing is considered or required

sections.title: Axial Load Tests
sections.body: Axial load tests are the most common type of drilled shaft load test. They can be conducted using conventional top-down static loading, bi-directional (O-cell) testing, rapid load testing (Statnamic), or high-strain dynamic methods. Planning, test method selection, instrumentation, and interpretation are all critical to obtaining reliable results that can be applied to production shaft design.
key_points: Four main test methods: conventional static, bi-directional, rapid, and dynamic
Selection depends on project requirements, available capacity, and budget
Proper planning and instrumentation are essential for meaningful results
sections.applicability: All axial load testing of drilled shafts

sections.title: Planning for Axial Load Tests
sections.body: Planning involves defining test objectives, selecting test shaft locations representative of production conditions, characterizing geomaterial properties at the test location, evaluating effects of scour, and determining construction methods. Prototype shafts (same size as production) are preferred over smaller trial shafts. Group effects and the potential need for multiple tests across variable conditions should be considered during planning.
key_points: Test objectives should be clearly defined before selecting methods
Test shafts should be located in representative subsurface conditions
Prototype (full-size) shafts are preferred over trial (reduced-size) shafts
Multiple tests may be needed where subsurface conditions vary significantly
Geotechnical investigation at the test shaft location is essential
sections.applicability: Planning phase for axial load test programs

sections.title: Test Methods for Axial Loading
sections.body: This section describes five categories of axial load tests: conventional top-down static, bi-directional (Osterberg cell), rapid load (Statnamic), high-strain dynamic (drop weight), and static uplift tests. Each method has specific advantages, limitations, and applicability depending on the magnitude of load, shaft geometry, subsurface conditions, and project budget.
key_points: Conventional static tests require reaction system capable of resisting test loads
Bi-directional tests use embedded hydraulic jack, eliminating external reaction
Rapid tests apply loads of 100-200 ms duration using combustion gases
High-strain dynamic tests use drop weights and wave equation analysis
sections.applicability: Selection of axial load test methods

sections.title: Conventional Top-Down Static Test
sections.body: Conventional static tests apply load in increments at the top of the shaft using hydraulic jacks reacting against a loaded platform, anchor piles, or ground anchors, following ASTM D1143 procedures. Load is applied in increments with settlements measured at each increment. The test continues until reaching the nominal resistance (plunging failure) or a specified displacement, typically 5% of shaft diameter. Cost and reaction capacity are the main limitations for large-diameter shafts.
key_points: Follows ASTM D1143 standard test procedures
Reaction system options: dead weight, anchor piles, ground anchors
Loading continued to 5% of shaft diameter displacement or plunging failure
Cost of reaction system may be prohibitive for shafts exceeding 20,000 kN capacity
Quick test method with 5-15 minute load increments is commonly used

sections.applicability: Static load testing of drilled shafts with available reaction capacity

sections.title: Bi-Directional (O-Cell) Test
sections.body: The bi-directional test uses one or more sacrificial hydraulic jacks (Osterberg cells) cast within the shaft. The jack loads upward against side resistance and downward against base resistance simultaneously. This method eliminates the need for an external reaction system and can test very large loads. Multi-level O-cell arrangements can be used to isolate side resistance in different strata. Results require construction of an equivalent top-loaded settlement curve.
key_points: O-cell is a sacrificial hydraulic jack cast into the shaft during construction
Eliminates need for external reaction system, enabling tests to very high loads
Multi-level arrangements can isolate resistance in different geologic strata
Equivalent top-loaded curve must be constructed from bi-directional results
Maximum test capacity limited by the lesser of side resistance above or base resistance below the cell
Horvath correction for side shear: delta_i = (delta_oc * L) / (2 * (E*A)_avg) (Eq 17-1)
equations: Eq 17-1: delta_i = (delta_oc * L) / (2 * (E*A)_avg) -- Horvath side shear correction
Eq 17-2: f_i = Q_i / (pi * D * delta_L_i) -- unit side resistance for O-cell segment

sections.applicability: Load testing of large-capacity drilled shafts, especially where external reaction is impractical

sections.title: Rapid Load Test (Statnamic)
sections.body: The Statnamic test applies a rapid compressive force using combustion of a propellant within a pressure chamber, generating a force pulse of 100-200 ms duration. The test measures force, acceleration, and displacement using a load cell and laser reference. Inertia and damping effects must be removed to obtain equivalent static resistance using the Unloading Point Method (UPM). Rate effect correction factors are applied: 0.96 for rock, 0.91 for sand, 0.69 for silt, and 0.65 for clay.
key_points: Force pulse duration of 100-200 ms from combustion of propellant
Measured force = static resistance + inertia force + damping force (Eq 17-3)
Unloading Point Method (UPM) used to derive equivalent static resistance
Rate effect factors: rock=0.96, sand=0.91, silt=0.69, clay=0.65
ASTM D7383 standard for rapid load testing
Test device mass approximately 5-10% of expected test load
equations: Eq 17-3: F_stn = F_static + c*v + m*a -- Statnamic force equilibrium
Eq 17-4: F_static = F_stn - c*v - m*a -- static resistance from Statnamic
Eq 17-5: F_derived_static = (1/eta) * F_static -- rate-corrected static resistance
tables: Table 17-1: Rate Effect Factors for Statnamic Tests (rock=0.96, sand=0.91, silt=0.69, clay=0.65)
sections.applicability: Rapid load testing of drilled shafts, particularly in cohesionless soils or rock

sections.title: High Strain Dynamic Test
sections.body: High-strain dynamic testing uses a drop weight impacting the shaft head, generating a stress wave analyzed by signal matching (CAPWAP). Strain gauges and accelerometers at the shaft top record force and velocity. The test requires calibration against static methods and is better suited for confirming minimum capacity than for precise capacity determination. It can be applied to production shafts as a proof test when other methods are not feasible.
key_points: Drop weight impact generates stress wave analyzed by CAPWAP signal matching
Strain gauges and accelerometers mounted near shaft top
Better suited for proof testing than precise capacity determination
ASTM D4945 standard applies (adapted from driven pile testing)
Drop height and weight must mobilize sufficient resistance
figures: Figure 17-10: Drop Weight Dynamic Test Setup
sections.applicability: Proof testing of drilled shaft capacity where static or bi-directional tests are not feasible

sections.title: Uplift Tests
sections.body: Static uplift tests apply tensile load to the shaft reinforcement to measure side resistance in tension. The test follows ASTM D3689 procedures. Results provide direct measurement of side resistance but require careful interpretation since the shaft concrete may crack under tension, affecting load distribution. The measured uplift resistance is typically less than the compressive side resistance due to Poisson effects reducing radial stress.
key_points: Follows ASTM D3689 standard procedures
Directly measures side resistance in tension
Tension side resistance is typically less than compression due to Poisson effects
Shaft concrete may crack under tension affecting load distribution
sections.applicability: Drilled shafts subject to uplift loads (transmission towers, anchorages)

sections.title: Instrumentation
sections.body: Instrumentation is essential for interpreting load test results beyond just total load-displacement behavior. Key measurements include applied load, shaft head displacement, load distribution along the shaft, and base displacement. Various instrument types are used including strain gauges (resistance, vibrating wire, fiber optic), telltales, extensometers, load cells, and accelerometers.
key_points: Instrumentation enables determination of load distribution along shaft
Strain gauges convert strain to load using estimated shaft stiffness (E*A)
Sister-bar vibrating wire strain gauges are the most common type
Fiber optic sensors emerging as alternative with continuous strain profiles
Redundancy in instrumentation is essential to guard against individual gauge failure
equations: Eq 17-6: Q_z = E*A*epsilon_z -- load at depth from strain
Eq 17-7: f_z = (Q_z1 - Q_z2) / (pi * D * delta_L) -- unit side resistance from load difference
Eq 17-8: E*A = Q_top / epsilon_top -- shaft composite stiffness from top measurements
Eq 17-9: SCR = (Q_z1 - Q_z2) / (gamma' * delta_L * pi * D) -- stress change ratio
figures: Figure 17-11: Vibrating Wire Sister-Bar Strain Gauge
Figure 17-12: Strain Gauge Installation on Reinforcing Cage
sections.applicability: Instrumentation planning for all types of drilled shaft load tests

sections.title: Interpretation of Results for Design
sections.body: Interpretation of load test results involves constructing load-settlement curves, determining nominal resistance, and deriving unit side resistance and base resistance for design. The 5% diameter criterion is used to define nominal resistance from the load-settlement curve. Results from bi-directional tests require construction of an equivalent top-loaded curve. For Statnamic tests, rate effect corrections are applied. Resistance factors per AASHTO for load-tested shafts range from 0.55 to 0.70 depending on site variability and test method.
key_points: Nominal resistance defined at displacement of 5% of shaft diameter
AASHTO resistance factors: 0.70 for static, 0.65 for Statnamic, 0.55 for dynamic
Site variability coefficient accounts for extrapolating test results to production shafts
Unit side resistance and base resistance derived from instrumented test data
Equivalent top-loaded curve construction required for bi-directional test results

sections.applicability: Applying load test results to production drilled shaft design

sections.title: Lateral Load Tests
sections.body: Lateral load tests measure the lateral load-displacement response of drilled shafts for calibration of p-y curve models used in design. These tests are particularly valuable for conditions where standard p-y models may not be reliable, such as rock sockets, weathered rock, cemented soils, or layered profiles. The test involves applying lateral load at or near ground level and measuring deflection and rotation at multiple points along the shaft.
key_points: Lateral tests calibrate p-y curve models for site-specific conditions
Particularly valuable for rock sockets and unusual geomaterial conditions
Both free-head and fixed-head boundary conditions can be tested
Inclinometer measurements provide deflection profile along shaft length
sections.applicability: Lateral load design of drilled shafts, especially in rock or unusual soil profiles

sections.title: Planning for Lateral Load Tests
sections.body: Planning for lateral load tests includes selecting shaft geometry representative of production conditions, determining the magnitude of lateral loads to be applied, and planning instrumentation. The reaction system can be another drilled shaft or a structural element. Inclinometer casings should be installed in the test shaft for measuring deflection profiles. Strain gauges at multiple levels enable derivation of bending moment profiles.
key_points: Test shaft geometry should match production shaft conditions
Inclinometer casings provide continuous deflection profiles
Strain gauges at multiple levels enable bending moment determination
Loading applied by hydraulic jack reacting against another shaft or structure
sections.applicability: Planning lateral load test programs for drilled shafts

sections.title: Test Methods for Lateral Loading
sections.body: Lateral load tests follow ASTM D3966 procedures. Load is applied in increments using a hydraulic jack reacting against an adjacent shaft or structure. Measurements include applied load, lateral displacement at multiple points on the shaft, and inclinometer readings. Rapid lateral load tests using Statnamic devices have also been developed. Cyclic lateral testing can evaluate performance under repeated loading conditions relevant to seismic or wave loading.
key_points: Follows ASTM D3966 standard procedures
Conventional reaction system uses paired shafts loaded against each other
Rapid lateral tests using Statnamic have been developed
Cyclic testing evaluates performance under repeated lateral loading
sections.applicability: Conducting lateral load tests on drilled shafts
